content:
Could we have a bot that warns with a post on the PR if any of the declarations introduced in it are already introduced in another existing PR? In #38938 (dualizing a file), at some point I had to resolve a conflict with master that was just deleting a lemma generated by @[to_dual] that someone else wrote explicitely because it was missing.

Not that the warning would have to be respected, but it could help give attention to the relevant PRs and avoid those merge conflicts.

Do you mean the same name or the same type? CI now produces a list of all declaration names so finding duplicate names across PRs is technically possible, but the same type with a different name would require more work / storage space.
I meant the same name, because I think those conflicts would arise more often for those small lemmas whose names are more or less unambiguous
Two PRs adding the same declaration happens very rarely these days (it was more common four years ago, when many basic things were missing), so I doubt adding an expensive check for that is worth it
A more interesting thing to look at is other PRs touching the same files. This also happens to be much cheaper to compute

I would actually really like something like this: I once had the experience of working on a series of PRs off and on for over a year only to find out that one of the key results I was proving was added in a separate PR ~halfway between when I started and when I finished.

It looks like in that case a bot that worked off of types would have caught the conflict, but one based off of names would not have, because I wasn't following the proper naming convention while I was working (perhaps that would have been less likely if there was a better linter for that, though).
The upstreaming dashboard already implements a variant of this idea (it doesn't compare two open PRs, but instead an open PR and files in your project's MyProject.Mathlib folder)
(this is one of the reasons I pushed so hard to get my upstreaming dashboard idea adopted by the community)
I agree, giving an easy way to see the open PRs touching the same files would probably be the right scope for this. Then, the author could decide if they are relevant by looking at the PRs themselves
